speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of the feeding difficulties and when the abdominal distension first became noticeable? I also need to know if the infant has had any episodes of vomiting or bile-stained stools.

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: I need to check if there are any signs of intestinal obstruction or infection. Are the stools normal in color and consistency, or have you noticed any blood, mucus, or significant changes in bowel movements?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has the infant ever passed a meconium stool within the first 48 hours of life, and have you noticed any explosive, foul-smelling watery stools or explosive diarrhea since then? REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_X-Ray

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, and radiological evidence of obstruction with an empty rectum, Hirschsprung disease is highly likely. REQUEST TEST: Rectal_Biopsy

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the biopsy was normal, Hirschsprung disease is ruled out. Have you noticed any respiratory symptoms like wheezing or recurrent infections, or any failure to thrive? REQUEST TEST: Sweat_Test

speaker: Doctor
text: Since Cystic Fibrosis and Hirschsprung disease are ruled out, I need to investigate other causes of lower intestinal obstruction. Has the infant had any episodes of painless rectal bleeding, often described as "currant jelly" stools, or has there been any intussusception suspected? REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_Ultrasound

speaker: Doctor
text: With Hirschsprung, CF, and intussusception ruled out, I am considering other causes of lower intestinal obstruction like meconium ileus equivalent or distal ileal atresia. Has the infant experienced any episodes of severe, crampy abdominal pain that resolve spontaneously, or any history of recurrent respiratory issues? REQUEST TEST: Contrast_Enema

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: A transition zone in the distal colon, compatible with Hirschsprung disease

speaker: Doctor
text: The contrast enema showing a transition zone is highly specific for Hirschsprung disease, suggesting the initial biopsy may have been a false negative due to sampling error. I will proceed with the diagnosis based on this confirmatory imaging evidence. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung disease
